scenes.kicker: F01 · Introduction to Financial Accounting · Module 1
scenes.head: The accounting equation
scenes.sub: Every business’s resources come from creditors or owners, so assets always equal liabilities plus equity. Learn to trace any transaction through that equation and to see how revenue, expenses and dividends change what the owners own.

segs.say: The accounting equation. Every business’s resources come from creditors or owners, so assets always equal liabilities plus equity. Learn to trace any transaction through that equation and to see how revenue, expenses and dividends change what the owners own.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: State the accounting equation and explain why it must balance after every transaction.
Analyse a business transaction into its effects on assets, liabilities and equity.
Use the expanded accounting equation to show how revenue, expenses and dividends change equity.
Distinguish contributed capital from retained earnings.
Calculate a missing element of the equation, including net income, from beginning and ending balances.

scenes.head: On 1 March 2026 Ana Lim opens a bank account for her new company, Lantern Coffee Co., and pays in $20,000 of her own savings.

segs.say: On 1 March 2026 Ana Lim opens a bank account for her new company, Lantern Coffee Co., and pays in $20,000 of her own savings. In exchange the company issues her shares of common stock. The same day the company borrows $10,000 from Coastline Bank. Lantern now holds $30,000 of cash. Ask where that cash came from and there are only two answers: $10,000 came from a lender, who expects to be repaid, and $20,000 came from the owner, who expects nothing back except a share of whatever the business becomes.

scenes.head: That is the whole idea of this lesson.

segs.say: That is the whole idea of this lesson. A business has resources, and every one of those resources was supplied by someone with a claim on it. Accounting records both sides of that fact: what the business has and who has a claim on it.

scenes.head: The resources are assets: things the business controls that are expected to bring it economic benefits, such as cash, equipment, supplies and amounts…

segs.say: The resources are assets: things the business controls that are expected to bring it economic benefits, such as cash, equipment, supplies and amounts customers owe it. The claims come in two kinds. Liabilities are what the business owes to outsiders: a bank loan, a supplier’s unpaid bill, a deposit for a service not yet delivered. Equity is the owners’ claim, and it is a residual claim: the owners are entitled to whatever is left of the assets after every liability has been settled.

scenes.head: Because the claims account for every dollar of resources, the two must be equal.

segs.say: Because the claims account for every dollar of resources, the two must be equal. This is the accounting equation:
Assets = Liabilities + Equity

scenes.head: It holds for a coffee cart, a hospital and a multinational, and it holds at every moment, not just at the end of the year.

segs.say: It holds for a coffee cart, a hospital and a multinational, and it holds at every moment, not just at the end of the year. It is not a rule that accountants enforce by adjusting numbers; it is true by construction, because equity is defined as what is left after liabilities. Rearranged, the equation says exactly that:
Equity = Assets − Liabilities

scenes.head: For this reason equity is often called net assets.

segs.say: For this reason equity is often called net assets. After its first day, Lantern has assets of $30,000, liabilities of $10,000 and equity of $20,000, and 30,000 = 10,000 + 20,000.

scenes.head: A transaction is an exchange or event that changes the business’s resources or the claims on them.

segs.say: A transaction is an exchange or event that changes the business’s resources or the claims on them. Because the equation must stay true, no transaction can change just one number. If assets go up, something else must also change: another asset goes down, a liability goes up, or equity goes up. This is the dual aspect of every transaction, and it is why the system you will learn in the next module is called double-entry bookkeeping.

scenes.head: Look at Lantern’s first week, transaction by transaction.

segs.say: Look at Lantern’s first week, transaction by transaction. For each one, ask two questions: which items changed, and in which direction?
Lantern’s first six transactions and their effect on the equation (fictional)

scenes.head: Three things in that table are worth slowing down for.

segs.say: Three things in that table are worth slowing down for. First, buying equipment partly for cash (3 March) changes three items, and the equation still balances because the asset gained ($12,000) equals the cash given up ($4,000) plus the new debt ($8,000). Second, paying for insurance in advance (4 March) changes no totals at all: one asset, cash, turns into another, the right to a year of insurance cover. Third, the deposit from Harbor Tech (8 March) brings in cash but is not income yet. Until Lantern caters the events, it owes Harbor Tech either the service or the money back, so the deposit is a liability called unearned revenue.

scenes.head: The test for any transaction

segs.say: The test for any transaction. Name what changed, say whether each item went up or down, and confirm that the change in assets equals the change in liabilities plus the change in equity. If it doesn’t, you have missed an effect or put one on the wrong side.

scenes.head: The equation rests on precise definitions, set by the bodies that write accounting standards.

segs.say: The equation rests on precise definitions, set by the bodies that write accounting standards. In the United States the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) defines an asset as “a present right of an entity to an economic benefit”, a liability as a present obligation to transfer an economic benefit, and equity as the residual interest in the assets after deducting liabilities (Concepts Statement No. 8, Chapter 4, issued December 2021). The International Accounting Standards Board (IASB), whose IFRS Accounting Standards are required in more than 140 jurisdictions, words it differently but builds the same structure: an asset is a present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events, a liability is a present obligation to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events, and equity is the residual interest (Conceptual Framework, March 2018).

scenes.head: US GAAP and IFRS

segs.say: US GAAP and IFRS. The two frameworks agree on the equation and on equity being a residual. They differ in wording and in some recognition rules elsewhere in the standards, which later courses cover. You will also meet different names for the same things: “stockholders’ equity” or “shareholders’ equity” in the United States, “share capital” for common stock and “statement of financial position” for the balance sheet under IFRS.

scenes.head: Two consequences of these definitions matter from the start.

segs.say: Two consequences of these definitions matter from the start. An item belongs on the asset side only if the business controls it and expects a benefit from it, so a loyal customer base or a talented barista, however valuable, is not recorded as an asset: the business neither owns nor controls them in the accounting sense. And a liability needs a present obligation, so a plan to buy a van next month is not a liability; nor is a signed order for one, until the van is delivered.

scenes.head: Equity changes for four reasons, and separating them tells a much richer story than one equity total.

segs.say: Equity changes for four reasons, and separating them tells a much richer story than one equity total. Owners can put money in, and they receive stock for it: that is contributed capital, recorded in Common Stock. The business can earn revenue by delivering goods or services, which increases equity. It incurs expenses in doing so, which decrease equity. And it can pay some of its profits back to the owners as dividends, which also decrease equity. Profit kept in the business accumulates in retained earnings. Putting the pieces into the equation gives the expanded accounting equation:
Assets = Liabilities + Common Stock + Retained Earnings_(beginning) + Revenue − Expenses − Dividends

scenes.head: Revenue minus expenses is net income for the period (a net loss if expenses are larger).

segs.say: Revenue minus expenses is net income for the period (a net loss if expenses are larger). At the end of the period, net income minus dividends is added to retained earnings, so the expanded equation collapses back into the basic one. Common stock is contributed capital; retained earnings are earned capital.

segs.say: Here is the rest of Lantern’s March, from 10 to 31 March, in the expanded form. Revenue, expenses and dividends now have their own columns inside equity.
Lantern’s remaining March transactions in the expanded equation (fictional)

scenes.head: At 31 March the expanded equation reads 43,150 = 21,160 + 20,000 + 0 + 5,700 − 3,410 − 300.

segs.say: At 31 March the expanded equation reads 43,150 = 21,160 + 20,000 + 0 + 5,700 − 3,410 − 300. Lantern began with no retained earnings, so the beginning balance is zero; net income for March, before adjustments, is 5,700 − 3,410 = 2,290.

scenes.head: Since a change in assets must equal the change in liabilities plus the change in equity, a transaction that touches two items can only follow one of…

segs.say: Since a change in assets must equal the change in liabilities plus the change in equity, a transaction that touches two items can only follow one of nine patterns. Recognising the pattern is the fastest way to check your analysis. Some transactions combine several patterns, as Lantern’s equipment purchase did.
Every two-sided transaction follows one of these patterns

chapters.title: When does something enter the equation?

scenes.head: Not every business event is a transaction.

segs.say: Not every business event is a transaction. On 20 March a hotel signs a contract with Lantern to cater its June conference for $5,000, payable after the event. Nothing has changed hands: Lantern hasn’t delivered any coffee and the hotel hasn’t paid anything. Each side has only promised to perform later, so Lantern records nothing yet. A contract like this, where neither party has performed, is called an executory contract, and it stays out of the equation until one side acts. If the hotel paid a deposit, Lantern would record cash and unearned revenue; when Lantern caters the conference, it records revenue.

scenes.head: The same test explains other non-events.

segs.say: The same test explains other non-events. Hiring a barista who starts next week creates no asset or liability today: wages become an expense, and a liability if unpaid, as the barista works. Placing an order for supplies that haven’t arrived and haven’t been paid for is a promise, not a transaction. What enters the equation is a change in resources or in obligations that already exist, measured reliably in money. This is why some important facts about a business, such as a large contract just signed or a key employee leaving, appear in the notes to the financial statements or not at all, rather than in the equation.

scenes.head: Measured in money, at a point in time

segs.say: Measured in money, at a point in time. The equation records only what can be measured in a currency (the monetary unit assumption) and only for this business, separate from its owners’ personal affairs (the economic entity assumption). Ana’s personal car is not Lantern’s asset unless she transfers it to the company, and her personal mortgage is not Lantern’s liability.

chapters.title: What a balanced equation does and doesn’t prove

scenes.head: A balanced equation proves that every recorded transaction affected both sides consistently.

segs.say: A balanced equation proves that every recorded transaction affected both sides consistently. It does not prove the records are right. If Lantern recorded its espresso machine as supplies, or forgot a transaction entirely, or recorded a $1,500 purchase as $150 on both sides, the equation would still balance. You will meet the same limitation again when you prepare a trial balance in lesson 7.

scenes.head: Nor does equity tell you what the business is worth.

segs.say: Nor does equity tell you what the business is worth. The amounts are mostly historical costs, what Lantern paid for things, and some valuable resources are not recorded at all. A buyer might pay far more, or far less, than Lantern’s $21,990 of equity (before the month-end adjustments). Equity is the owners’ accounting claim, not a market price and not a pile of cash: Lantern’s equity is spread across cash, equipment, supplies and what customers owe.

scenes.head: Sole proprietors and partnerships

segs.say: Sole proprietors and partnerships. Lantern is a corporation, so owners’ investments are recorded as Common Stock and payments to them as Dividends. In a business owned by one person without incorporating, the same ideas use an owner’s capital account and withdrawals (also called drawings). The equation is identical.

scenes.head: The accounting equation

segs.say: The accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Equity.
Assets: Resources the business controls that are expected to bring economic benefits ($).
Liabilities: Present obligations to transfer resources to outsiders ($).
Equity: The owners’ residual claim on the assets ($).
It assumes this: All three are measured at the same moment, in the same currency.
True after every transaction, because equity is defined as assets minus liabilities.

scenes.head: Equity as net assets

segs.say: Equity as net assets: Equity = Assets − Liabilities.
Equity: The residual claim: what would be left for owners after every liability is settled at book amounts ($).
Use it to find any one element when the other two are known.

scenes.head: The expanded accounting equation

segs.say: The expanded accounting equation: A = L + CS + RE_(beg) + R − E − D.
A, L: Assets and liabilities at the end of the period ($).
CS: Common stock: capital contributed by owners ($).
RE_(beg): Retained earnings at the start of the period ($).
R, E: Revenue and expenses for the period ($).
D: Dividends declared in the period ($).
It assumes this: Revenue, expenses and dividends are the period’s totals, not yet moved into retained earnings.

scenes.head: Net income

segs.say: Net income: Net income = Revenue − Expenses.
Net income: Profit for the period; negative means a net loss ($).
Dividends are not expenses and are not subtracted here.

scenes.head: Retained earnings at the end of a period

segs.say: Retained earnings at the end of a period: RE_(end) = RE_(beg) + Net income − Dividends.
RE_(end): Profit kept in the business since it began, at the end of the period ($).

chapters.title: Example: Lantern after its first three transactions

scenes.head: Lantern after its first three transactions

segs.say: Lantern issues $20,000 of common stock for cash, borrows $10,000 from the bank, then buys $12,000 of equipment, paying $4,000 in cash and owing the supplier $8,000. What are total assets, liabilities and equity, and does the equation balance?

scenes.head: Lantern after its first three transactions

segs.say: Step 1. Stock issue: cash (an asset) rises by $20,000 and common stock (equity) rises by $20,000. Pattern: asset up, equity up.
Step 2. Bank loan: cash rises by $10,000 and notes payable (a liability) rises by $10,000. Pattern: asset up, liability up.

Step 3. Equipment purchase: equipment rises by $12,000 and cash falls by $4,000, so assets rise by a net $8,000; accounts payable rises by $8,000. Change in assets 8,000 = change in liabilities 8,000 + change in equity 0.
Step 4. Add up. Assets: cash 20,000 + 10,000 − 4,000 = 26,000, plus equipment 12,000, makes 38,000. Liabilities: 10,000 + 8,000 = 18,000. Equity: 20,000.

scenes.head: Lantern after its first three transactions

segs.say: Assets $38,000 = liabilities $18,000 + equity $20,000.

Lantern controls $38,000 of resources. Lenders and a supplier have claims on $18,000 of them and Ana, as owner, on the remaining $20,000. Buying the equipment didn’t make her any richer or poorer: it changed what the business holds and whom it owes.

chapters.title: Example: Finding net income from the equation

scenes.head: Finding net income from the equation

segs.say: Kestrel Battery Installers, a fictional company that fits home battery-storage systems, began the year with assets of $480,000 and liabilities of $300,000. During the year it issued $50,000 of new common stock and paid $20,000 of dividends. At the end of the year its assets were $610,000 and its liabilities $370,000. What was its net income for the year?

scenes.head: Finding net income from the equation

segs.say: Step 1. Equity at the start: 480,000 − 300,000 = 180,000.
Step 2. Equity at the end: 610,000 − 370,000 = 240,000. So equity rose by 60,000 during the year.
Step 3. List what moves equity: new stock adds 50,000, net income adds an unknown NI, dividends subtract 20,000. So 60,000 = 50,000 + NI − 20,000.

scenes.head: Finding net income from the equation

segs.say: Net income was $30,000.

Assets grew by $130,000, but most of that growth was paid for by new debt ($70,000) and new owners’ money ($50,000). Only $30,000 came from profit, and two-thirds of it was paid out as dividends. Reading the change in equity this way separates growth that was earned from growth that was financed.

chapters.title: Example: Can Lantern borrow for a van?

scenes.head: Can Lantern borrow for a van?

segs.say: After its month-end adjustments, Lantern’s balance sheet at 31 March shows assets of $42,500, liabilities of $21,810 and equity of $20,690. Ana wants to borrow $15,000 to buy a delivery van. The bank lends only if, after the loan, total liabilities are no more than 1.5 times equity. Does the loan fit, and if not, what are her options?

scenes.head: Can Lantern borrow for a van?

segs.say: Step 1. The loan adds $15,000 of cash (soon a van) to assets and $15,000 to liabilities; equity is unchanged. Liabilities become 21,810 + 15,000 = 36,810; assets become 57,500.
Step 2. The bank’s limit is 1.5 × 20,690 = 31,035 of liabilities. With 36,810 Lantern would be over the limit; the ratio would be 36,810 ÷ 20,690 ≈ 1.78.
Step 3. Option A, borrow less: the most Lantern can add is 31,035 − 21,810 = 9,225.
Step 4. Option B, add equity first: Ana buys more stock for cash, raising equity by x. The loan fits if 36,810 ≤ 1.5(20,690 + x), so x ≥ 36,810 ÷ 1.5 − 20,690 = 3,850.

scenes.head: Can Lantern borrow for a van?

segs.say: The full $15,000 loan breaks the bank’s condition. Lantern can borrow up to $9,225, or Ana can invest at least $3,850 more in exchange for stock and then borrow the full $15,000.

Lenders watch the equation because equity is their cushion: the larger it is relative to liabilities, the more the business could lose before creditors go unpaid. The new owner’s money in option B also increases assets, which is why it reassures the bank. You will study ratios like this one properly in F03.

scenes.head: “Revenue means cash came in.”

segs.say: “Revenue means cash came in.”. Revenue is earned when the business delivers the service, whether or not it has been paid. Lantern’s $4,200 conference invoice is revenue on 12 March although no cash arrived until later; Harbor Tech’s $2,400 deposit is cash but not revenue, because the events haven’t happened. Ask “has the business done what it was paid for?”, not “has money arrived?”.

scenes.head: “Dividends are an expense.”

segs.say: “Dividends are an expense.”. Dividends reduce equity, but they are a distribution of profit to owners, not a cost of earning revenue. They are left out of net income and subtracted from retained earnings afterwards. Treating them as an expense would make Lantern’s March profit look $300 smaller than it was.

scenes.head: “Paying a bill is an expense.”

segs.say: “Paying a bill is an expense.”. When Lantern pays the $1,000 it owes for supplies, assets and liabilities both fall and equity doesn’t move. The cost was recorded when the supplies were bought (as an asset) and becomes an expense when they are used. Paying the bill only settles the debt.

scenes.head: “Equity is the owner’s money in the bank.”

segs.say: “Equity is the owner’s money in the bank.”. Equity is a claim on all the assets, not a particular asset. Lantern’s $21,990 of equity at 31 March, before adjustments, is spread across cash, equipment, insurance cover, supplies and receivables. Nor is it a market value: someone buying Lantern would pay what they think its future is worth.

scenes.head: “If the equation balances, the records are correct.”

segs.say: “If the equation balances, the records are correct.”. The equation catches one-sided mistakes only. Recording equipment as supplies, omitting a transaction, or entering the same wrong amount on both sides all leave it balanced. Balancing is necessary, not sufficient.

scenes.head: Lenders read the equation first.

segs.say: Lenders read the equation first. When Ana asks Coastline Bank for more credit, the loan officer looks at how much of Lantern’s assets is financed by owners compared with creditors, because the owners’ equity absorbs losses before the bank does. Loan agreements often turn this into a covenant, a condition such as “total liabilities may not exceed 1.5 times equity”, and checking it means working the equation forward for the planned borrowing, exactly as in the applied example.

scenes.head: Investors and owners read the change in equity, not just its level.

segs.say: Investors and owners read the change in equity, not just its level. Kestrel’s equity grew by $60,000, but only $30,000 of that was earned. A business can grow its assets quickly by borrowing or by raising money from new shareholders; the expanded equation shows how much of the growth came from profitable operations, which is the part that can continue without more outside money.

scenes.head: Managers use the dual aspect as a planning check.

segs.say: Managers use the dual aspect as a planning check. Before Lantern commits to a $15,000 van, Ana can write the transaction into the equation and see its consequences: cash rises, then turns into a vehicle; a liability appears that must be repaid with interest; equity is untouched until the van starts earning revenue and costing fuel and depreciation. Financial models built in spreadsheets include a “balance check” row for the same reason: if projected assets ever differ from projected liabilities plus equity, the model has an error, and analysts don’t trust its numbers until it balances.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: Assets = liabilities + equity, at every moment, because equity is defined as what is left of the assets after liabilities.
Every transaction changes at least two items, and the change in assets always equals the change in liabilities plus the change in equity.
Equity grows when owners invest or the business earns revenue, and shrinks with expenses and dividends: A = L + CS + RE(beginning) + R − E − D.
Net income is revenue minus expenses; dividends are not expenses. Ending retained earnings = beginning retained earnings + net income − dividends.
Cash and revenue are different things: a deposit for future work is a liability, and work invoiced on credit is revenue before any cash arrives.
A balanced equation proves consistency, not correctness, and equity is an accounting claim, not the market value of the business.
